summary: This RFC discusses how sites with several local links behind one gateway might organize them as subnets of an Internet network. It proposes a standard way of subnetting so the rest of the Internet need not care about internal details.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo proposes one way to divide a site's network into subnets while keeping that internal structure hidden from the rest of the Internet. A host uses a mask to decide whether a destination is on its own subnet.

questions: toward an internet standard for subnetting
how should sites organize local links as subnets
how does a host decide if a destination is on its subnet
subtitle: A proposed subnetting scheme that uses a mask to guide local routing decisions.

tldr.problem: Hosts in subnetted networks need compatible rules for deciding whether a datagram is local or must go to a gateway.
tldr.mechanism: The scheme takes subnet bits from the host portion of an address and describes a 32-bit mask test for local destinations.
tldr.outcome: Subnetting remains a local choice; the memo strongly recommends its scheme when subnetting is used.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 940 an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text discusses a proposed standard scheme for subnetting.

sections.title: Why a Common Subnet Scheme Matters
sections.content:
A site may have several local links connected to the Internet through a gateway. Subnetting treats each link as a network-like entity and uses subgateways, bridges, or gateways to connect them.

Hosts must decide whether to send a datagram directly on a local subnet or through a gateway. A standard scheme matters because hosts from different suppliers may otherwise fail to work together.
sections.plainLanguage: A host needs one consistent rule to decide whether a destination is nearby or needs a gateway. Without a shared rule, equipment from different suppliers may not interoperate.

sections.title: Adding a Subnet Field
sections.content:
The address structure has a network field and a per-network rest field. The proposal adds an optional subnet field by taking bits from the rest, or host, field. The subnet details are site-specific, and networks of classes A, B, and C may use subnets.

A site uses one IP network number and appears as one network from outside. The memo does not require a particular host implementation and does not specify how routing itself is done.
sections.plainLanguage: A site can use part of its host-address space to label local subnets. Outside the site, the whole group still appears as one network.

sections.title: The 32-Bit Mask Test
sections.content:
The example host uses a 32-bit mask and its own IP address. If the masked destination address equals the masked local address, the host assumes the destination is on its subnet; otherwise it sends the datagram to a gateway.

The mask may be configured at boot or distributed by a protocol outside this memo. The procedure applies separately to each interface on a multihomed host. The memo cites RFC 917 for background and rationale.
sections.plainLanguage: The host compares the parts of its address and the destination selected by the mask. A match means local delivery; a difference means use a gateway.

references.text: Postel, J., "Multi-LAN Address Resolution", RFC-925, October 1984.
